pr_title: Reduce the likelihood of writing small segments due to an oversize translog.
pr_body:
Configuring the maximum size that a translog might take is hard: make it too
high and recoveries might take a very long time, make it too low and the engine
will keep writing tiny segments and add merging overhead. 

Currently, every shard has a budget of 512MB that they may spend on their
transaction log. When playing with the TSDB Rally track on my local machine, this
boils down to flushing every ~4 seconds when the indexing buffer only collected
~60MB of data (compared to a total capacity of 10%*4GB=410MB on a 4GB heap).
This frequent flushing adds significant pressure on merging. Ideally, a node
that would want to max out ingestion rate would write segments because it hit
the memory budget of the indexing buffer, not the disk budget of the translog.

This change proposes to increase the size threshold of the translog to 10GB, or
~20% of the recommended shard size, which should help ensure that the space
overhead of translog remains somewhat under control. In addition to a size
threshold, it adds an age threshold that default to 1 minute. This age
threshold aims at controlling the maximum time that a recovery may take and has
the good property of allowing shards that are heavily ingested into to consume
more translog if it helps. In contrast, shards that receive little indexing would
flush much more frequently than every 512MB of data.

On top of this, there is an optimization in `InternalEngine#writeIndexingBuffer`
to a flush instead of a refresh if we are more than halfway through either of
the thresholds. This helps avoid doing a flush to reclaim translog disk space
shortly after doing a refresh to reclaim indexing buffer memory.

Closes #75611

A few observations:
 - Much less refreshing, flushing and merging. I confirmed through logging that refresh() is now mostly called to clear the indexing buffer, every ~410MB of indexing buffer and every ~4GB of translog.
 - When combining the indexing, refreshing, flushing and merging times, overally CPU time decreased by 15%.
 - High percentiles of service times for indexing requests increased, because writing segments happens on indexing threads.
 - The ingestion rate is not improved. One reason is because I'm running with 16 clients to preserve indexing order while my machine has 24 threads, which has the side-effect of reserving some threads for merging.

Same track with same parameters except the number of indexing clients: 32 instead of 16 in order to make indexing and merging compete for the same resources (as expected). This yielded a 7% indexing throughput improvement.

Thanks @henningandersen for looking. I confirmed that a 1 minute interval still helps significantly reduce the flush and merge times, which makes sense to me since I was previously observing flushes every ~4 seconds, so it's still about one order of magnitude fewer flushes. I also applied your suggestion to take total disk space into account and actually went a bit further than what you suggested by enforcing that a translog may not use more than 1% of the total disk space.

I checked how translogs affect refreshes on the Logging track. This track is a bit helped by the fact that indexing operations go to multiple indices, and the size of the translog is per shard. That said, application logs get most of the indexing load, and on my machine the translog size threshold forces refreshes every 9 seconds on the single-shard index that holds application logs. So trying to move the interval between flushes closer to 60 seconds with this change should help relieve the merging pressure there too.

issue_context.title: index.translog.flush_threshold_size is too small for large nodes to use their entire indexing buffer
issue_context.body:
I ran the `solutions/logs` track, which indexes concurrently into 13 data streams with different indexing rates, with 3 shards / 1 replica per data stream, the default refresh interval, no concurrent searches, on a cluster that consisted of 3 i3 instances with 30GB of heap each.

Given that this benchmark never refreshes the shards, I was expecting that the index writer buffers would get written to disk when they hit the limit of 10% of the node heap, 3GB of heap with these instances. However in practice the index writer buffers almost always got written to disk because of `index.translog.flush_threshold_size`, which controls the maximum size of the translog and has a default value of 512MB. When the translog hits this size, the shard gets flushed, which also happens to flush the indexing buffer.

I ran the benchmark again with a `index.translog.flush_threshold_size` of 5GB to see if that changed anything, and I could indeed see several occurrences of `IndexingMemoryController` flushing the content of the indexing buffer to disk before reaching the maximum translog flush threshold.

In this case, this only marginally improved the indexing rate (+1%) but the number of merges (-65%) and the amount of time spent merging (-36%) are noticeably lower despite a lower segment count (-14%).

Since this problem doesn't translate into a significantly slower indexing rate, there is a question of whether this is actually a problem. In this case it wasn't, but we also have data structures that are costly merging-wise, e.g. multi-dimensional points that are used by geo points, geo shapes and range fields need to recompute the entire BKD tree upon merge. And likewise the new data structure for vector search that gets introduced in Lucene 9 also recomputes the data structure entirely upon merges.

I'm not sure what's the best way to address this, increasing the default flush threshold also has bad implications e.g. on transient disk usage with many shards. But maybe there are other approaches we could take like scaling the translog flush size to the indexing rate of the shard or to the total amount of disk of the node like we do for the indexing buffer, adding lightweight compression to the translog, ...
comments:
I think the main trade-off here is the issues you identified (small segments, more merging) vs translog disk usage and recovery time. I am particularly worried about the latter, which I think could be several minutes with a 5GB translog. We could parallellize here and also limiting the cumulated translog size on a node could help keep the total recovery time of a node at bay.

I wonder if an alternative is to use the [merge-on-commit/refresh](https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/LUCENE-8962) functionality in lucene? Clearly depends on the overhead of it.

Another option is to allow lucene to keep state and flush full segments including data previously flushed, discarding the previous segment for every commit up until a threshold. In this specific case it looks like that would have around a 1% overhead on indexing (back of an envelope calculation). But the merge-on-commit/refresh might work better and would also help when searches/refreshes do occur.

@jpountz and I discussed this with following outcome (correct me if I am misremembering, Adrien):

1. Adrien clarified that merge-on-commit only waits for a merge to complete more than it actually includes previous segments in the commit.
2. We discussed the full-flush idea and agreed that based on the numbers that should lead to less than a 1% overhead. This will require lucene changes.
3. We discussed another idea to let a refresh that happens when translog is say more than 80% full convert into a flush to avoid first refreshing and then flushing.
4. We need a benchmark that provokes an actual performance difference before proceeding.

Another idea we discussed consists of managing the disk budget of the translog on a per-node basis rather than a per-shard basis, similarly to how IndexingMemoryController manages the IndexWriter RAM buffer size at the node level.

Another data point I just captured: changing the flush size of the translog from 512MB to 5GB significantly reduced merging activity on the TSDB track on my local machine with a 4GB heap for Elasticsearch.

I was interested in checking this out with TSDB, because it typically indexes less than other datasets (metrics only have doc values) so it consumes little IndexWriter buffer, and it is very space-efficient: documents are stored much more efficiently in the index than in the translog. 

```

|                      Cumulative merge count of primary shards |                         |   920           |   250           |  -670       |        |  -72.83% |
```

review_comments: This seems to be primarily a safety net to catch cases where the time-based flush (or memory controller flush) does not keep the size at bay. For very small instances, like 1GB RAM, 30 GB disk, this higher bound seems high and could maybe be a degradation for edge cases (heavy updates). I suggest to make it something like `min(available_disk/10, 10GB)`.

I think this is good but want to point out that it assumes the defaults are in play and that the system is not memory constrained.

For a memory constrained system with manual tuning of flush size threshold, this could lead to 2x more flushes than expected (first doing several refreshes, then a flush at half the desired size).

In my opinion this is fine, seems like an edge case and even then, then impact is hopefully not enormous.
Agreed, I'll improve the comment to make it more explicit. Hopefully this becomes a bit less of a concern when we write a single segment to reclaim memory instead of writing all pending segments.
